Sinful
SIN-ful
adj.
From sin, Saxon synn, and the suffix -ful. Webster 1828: tainted with sin; wicked; iniquitous; criminal; and, of things, containing or proceeding from sin. The word describes a nature as well as an act.

Biblical Definition

Sinful in Scripture describes a nation, a generation, a man, and sin itself. Isaiah opens his prophecy with the nation: Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward (Isaiah 1:4) — four descriptions and then four verbs, addressed not to pagans but to Judah. The Lord uses it of the age in which His disciples must confess Him: Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation (Mark 8:38). Peter uses it of himself, at the moment he had most reason to be pleased with a large catch of fish: When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord (Luke 5:8) — the nearer Christ comes, the more the man sees. And Paul uses it of sin itself, describing what the law accomplishes: that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful (Romans 7:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SINFUL as tainted with sin; wicked; iniquitous; criminal; unholy; and, applied to actions or things, containing sin or proceeding from a corrupt nature.

expand to see more

SINFUL, a. — Tainted with sin; wicked; iniquitous; criminal; unholy.

Containing sin, or consisting in sin; as, a sinful action or a sinful thought.

Proceeding from a corrupt nature; as, sinful desires or sinful affections.

SIN, n. — The voluntary departure of a moral agent from a known rule of rectitude prescribed by God.

From Saxon synn, sin, and -ful, full of — the root also of sinner and sinless.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 1:4 — "Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward."

Mark 8:38 — "Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."

Luke 5:8 — "When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord."

Romans 7:13 — "Was then that which is good made death unto me? God forbid. But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful."

Modern Corruption

Romans 7:13 says the law was given so that sin might appear as sin and become exceeding sinful, which is exactly the office the modern pulpit has retired by preaching grace without ever preaching law.

expand to see more

Paul’s argument is that the commandment does not create sin but exposes it: I had not known sin, but by the law: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet (Romans 7:7). The law functions like light in a dark room, and its effect is to make sin appear sin and become exceeding sinful. The Reformed tradition calls this the pedagogical use of the law, and Galatians 3:24 says it is a schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ. A ministry that never preaches the commandments is not thereby more gracious; it leaves hearers with no measure of their condition and therefore no felt need of a Saviour, which is why so much modern conversion is shallow. Antinomianism and legalism are both errors about the law’s use, and the answer to each is the same: the law cannot justify, and it must be preached.

Luke 5:8 shows what the law’s work looks like when it lands. Peter had just had the best morning’s fishing of his life, given him by Christ after a night of nothing, and his response was not gratitude but terror: Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord. The nearer Christ came, the plainer his own condition became — the same reaction as Isaiah’s Woe is me! for I am undone and John’s falling as dead at His feet. Isaiah 1:4 shows the corporate version, and its address should be noted: Ah sinful nation is spoken to the covenant people, not to Babylon, and the chapter continues with God saying He is weary of their sacrifices. Self-knowledge of this kind is the first work of grace, not an obstacle to it, and the Lord’s answer to Peter was Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chata (H2398), to miss the mark, to sin; chattath (H2403), sin, a sin offering; Greek hamartia (G266), sin, a missing of the mark; hamartolos (G268), a sinner.

expand to see more

Hebrew chata (H2398) — to miss, to fail of a goal; the basic Old Testament verb for sinning.

Hebrew chattath (H2403) — sin, and also the sin offering; the same word for the offence and the remedy.

Greek hamartia (G266) — a missing of the mark, sin; exceeding sinful is hamartolos beyond measure (Romans 7:13).

Greek hamartolos (G268) — sinful, a sinner; I am a sinful man, O Lord (Luke 5:8).

Greek hyperbole (G5236) — excess, beyond measure; the exceeding of Romans 7:13, whence the English hyperbole.

Usage

"Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity (Isaiah 1:4) — spoken to the covenant people, not to Babylon."

"Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord (Luke 5:8) — the nearer Christ comes, the more the man sees."

"That sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful (Romans 7:13) — the law as light in a dark room."
